payload.title: Poetry Analysis: Mending Wall
payload.set_intro:
Public-domain source text — Robert Frost, Mending Wall, North of Boston (London: David Nutt, 1914)
Mending Wall
by Robert Frost
The following poem is by Robert Frost (1914).

```passage
SOMETHING there is that doesn't love a wall,
That sends the frozen-ground-swell under it,
And spills the upper boulders in the sun;
And makes gaps even two can pass abreast.
The work of hunters is another thing:
I have come after them and made repair
Where they have left not one stone on a stone,
But they would have the rabbit out of hiding,
To please the yelping dogs. The gaps I mean,
No one has seen them made or heard them made,
But at spring mending-time we find them there.
I let my neighbour know beyond the hill;
And on a day we meet to walk the line
And set the wall between us once again.
We keep the wall between us as we go.
To each the boulders that have fallen to each.
And some are loaves and some so nearly balls
We have to use a spell to make them balance:
"Stay where you are until our backs are turned!"
We wear our fingers rough with handling them.
Oh, just another kind of out-door game,
One on a side. It comes to little more:
There where it is we do not need the wall:
He is all pine and I am apple orchard.
My apple trees will never get across
And eat the cones under his pines, I tell him.
He only says, "Good fences make good neighbours."
Spring is the mischief in me, and I wonder
If I could put a notion in his head:
"Why do they make good neighbours? Isn't it
Where there are cows? But here there are no cows.
Before I built a wall I'd ask to know
What I was walling in or walling out,
And to whom I was like to give offence.
Something there is that doesn't love a wall,
That wants it down." I could say "Elves" to him,
But it's not elves exactly, and I'd rather
He said it for himself. I see him there
Bringing a stone grasped firmly by the top
In each hand, like an old-stone savage armed.
He moves in darkness as it seems to me,
Not of woods only and the shade of trees.
He will not go behind his father's saying,
And he likes having thought of it so well
He says again, "Good fences make good neighbours."
```

parts.label: A
parts.prompt:
The following poem is "Mending Wall" by Robert Frost (1914). In this poem, the speaker describes the yearly spring job of rebuilding a stone wall with his neighbor and thinks about why the two of them keep it.

Read the poem closely. Then write an essay in which you analyze how Robert Frost uses poetic elements and techniques to convey the speaker's divided attitude toward the wall, which he mocks as needless yet calls his neighbor to rebuild every year, and toward the neighbor, whose inherited certainty he both looks down on and cannot shake.

Your essay should:
- Respond to the prompt with a thesis that offers a defensible interpretation of the poem.
- Use specific evidence from the poem, and explain how that evidence supports your line of reasoning.
- Explain how multiple poetic elements and techniques contribute to the meaning you describe.
- Write clearly, with appropriate grammar and punctuation.
parts.model_answer:
In "Mending Wall," Robert Frost's speaker spends most of the poem making fun of a wall that he himself calls his neighbor out to repair every spring. That contradiction is the center of the poem. Through quiet irony, the playful language of games and spells, and a late turn toward darker imagery, Frost presents a speaker who sees himself as the free thinker of the pair but who is just as tied to the wall as his neighbor is. In the end his teasing works as a wall of its own.

The poem opens with a riddle instead of a statement: "Something there is that doesn't love a wall" (line 1). The inverted syntax holds back the subject and makes the line sound like an old country saying. That mysterious "Something," which "sends the frozen-ground-swell under it," gives nature a will, and the speaker clearly sides with it. Only a few lines later, though, he admits, "I let my neighbour know beyond the hill" (12). The flat, plain wording of this line is the irony. The man who seems to be on the side of the gaps is the one who sets up the repair. Frost doesn't point this out. He just puts the two ideas close together and lets the reader see the gap between them. The repeated phrase "between us" in lines 14 and 15 sharpens the point, because the two men are working side by side and sharing a "we" even as the wall they are building keeps them apart.

The speaker handles this tension by turning the work into play. He calls it "just another kind of out-door game, / One on a side" (21-22), which makes the hard labor of lifting boulders sound like a sport with teams. Even his spell, "Stay where you are until our backs are turned!" (19), is half a joke, but it also shows him joining in a ritual instead of standing outside it. When he finally argues, his logic is concrete and a little smug: "He is all pine and I am apple orchard" (24). The neighbor answers with a proverb, and the speaker blames his own urge to question on the season, saying "Spring is the mischief in me" (28). Calling it mischief rather than conviction lets him avoid committing to his own argument. Most of his challenge is something he only wonders about saying, and he holds back the word "Elves" because he would "rather / He said it for himself" (37-38). So he wants the neighbor to tear down the wall, but he won't say so plainly himself.

The playfulness disappears near the end. The speaker sees his neighbor holding a stone in each hand "like an old-stone savage armed" (40). With this simile the neighbor stops being a partner in a game and becomes a primitive fighter, and the stones turn into weapons. The image of darkness goes further: "He moves in darkness as it seems to me, / Not of woods only" (41-42). The literal shade of the pines becomes a metaphor for ignorance, and "his father's saying" (43) suggests that the neighbor's certainty was handed down to him, not thought out. Still, the hedge "as it seems to me" admits that this judgment is only the speaker's view, and the condescension says as much about him as it does about the neighbor.

What keeps the poem from being a simple victory for the speaker is that he has his own refrain too. He repeats "Something there is that doesn't love a wall" in line 35, and it sounds as inherited and as unexplained as "Good fences make good neighbours." He mocks blind repetition while doing it himself. Frost also gives the neighbor the last line, and the proverb stands with no answer. The speaker never really wins the argument, because he never fully makes it. His division is left unresolved. He resents the wall, looks down on the man who believes in it, and still meets him at the line every spring.

rubric_rows.criterion: A defensible thesis must say something about the speaker's divided or complicated attitude, toward the wall, the neighbor, or both, and should hint at how the poem shows that division. Good examples: the speaker questions the wall yet starts the repair every year, or his teasing hides a fear of the neighbor's closed, inherited thinking. A thesis does not earn the point if it only says the poem is about walls or barriers, only says the speaker is against the wall and the neighbor is for it, or only lists devices with no claim about attitude. The thesis may appear anywhere in the essay but must be clear and arguable.

Strong responses use specific evidence and explain how it shows the speaker's divided stance. Key evidence: the personified 'Something' that 'doesn't love a wall'; the irony that 'I let my neighbour know'; the shared work and the repeated 'between us'; calling the job 'just another kind of out-door game'; the half-serious 'spell' and the 'Elves' he won't quite name; the pine and apple contrast; the 'old-stone savage armed' simile and the 'darkness' image; and the neighbor's repeated proverb, which frames the end of the poem. A 4 links several of these to a line of reasoning that traces how the attitude changes, for example from playful rule-following to sharper judgment once the neighbor is seen as 'armed' and moving 'in darkness.' A 3 explains relevant evidence but unevenly. A 2 mostly summarizes or names devices with thin commentary. A 1 offers little more than restatement.

Sophistication can be shown by exploring tension that the poem leaves unresolved. Examples: the speaker who mocks 'his father's saying' is himself relying on a saying ('Something there is') and on a 'spell.' The speaker's teasing is a kind of wall of its own, since he would 'rather / He said it for himself' and never says his question out loud. The neighbor's proverb gets the last word, and the poem lets it stand without refuting it. An essay can also earn the point by weighing the gap between the speaker's warmth in the shared work and his condescension in the 'savage' simile. Merely mentioning that walls can be both good and bad, or adding outside political allegory, does not earn the point unless it is grounded in the text and sustained.

Sample essay (mid; scored 4/6: thesis 1, evidence 3, sophistication 0)
In "Mending Wall," Robert Frost shows a speaker who is of two minds. He makes fun of the wall and of his neighbor, but he is also the one who calls the neighbor every spring to fix it, so he is part of the thing he questions. Frost uses personification, tone, and imagery to show this divided attitude, which gets sharper toward the end of the poem.

The poem begins by saying "Something there is that doesn't love a wall." This is personification, since the force that knocks the wall down is given feelings, and it makes it seem like nature itself is on the speaker's side against the wall. The line is repeated later, which shows the speaker keeps coming back to this idea. But right after, the speaker says "I let my neighbour know beyond the hill." This is ironic because he is the one who starts the mending. He complains about the wall, but he still keeps it going each year, so he does not fully believe his own argument.

The speaker also treats the work as playful. He calls it "just another kind of out-door game," and he uses a "spell" to make the stones balance. These details make the tone light and teasing, and they show he enjoys working with his neighbor even though he thinks the wall is pointless. The phrase "between us" is repeated, which shows that the wall separates them but they are also doing the job together. The contrast between "pine" and "apple orchard" is used to prove his point that the wall is not needed, since his trees will never bother the neighbor's.

However, the tone changes near the end. When the speaker sees the neighbor "like an old-stone savage armed," the simile is not friendly anymore. It makes the neighbor seem primitive and a little dangerous. The speaker also says the neighbor "moves in darkness," which is an image that suggests the neighbor is not thinking clearly, only following what he was taught. The speaker looks down on him for this. But the speaker never actually says his question out loud, saying he would "rather he said it for himself," so he is holding back too.

The poem ends with the neighbor repeating "Good fences make good neighbours," the same line from before. Because it is repeated, it feels like the neighbor has the final word and the speaker does not answer him. This shows the speaker cannot fully shake the neighbor's certainty even though he thinks he is smarter. In the end, Frost uses these techniques to show that the speaker is both against the wall and part of it, and that he is both amused by his neighbor and bothered by him.
- Row A: "he is also the one who calls the neighbor every spring to fix it, so he is part of the thing he questions" - Defensible thesis: it names the speaker's divided attitude (mocks the wall yet starts the repair) and previews the techniques. It is somewhat general about how the poem shows the division, but it answers the prompt, so it earns the thesis point.
- Row B: "This is personification, since the force that knocks the wall down is given feelings" - Names a technique and gives a specific quotation, with some explanation of effect (nature on the speaker's side). The commentary is brief and does not tie the personification closely to the speaker's ambivalence.
- Row B: "This is ironic because he is the one who starts the mending." - Uses a key piece of evidence ("I let my neighbour know") and explains how it shows the speaker undercutting his own argument. This is good, relevant commentary, though it stays at one sentence of analysis.
- Row B: "These details make the tone light and teasing, and they show he enjoys working with his neighbor" - Evidence from "game" and "spell" is used, but the commentary is general ("light and teasing") and does not explore how the half-serious spell connects to the Elves or to the speaker's own reliance on sayings. The pine and apple point is only summarized.
- Row B: "the simile is not friendly anymore. It makes the neighbor seem primitive and a little dangerous." - Good identification of a shift in attitude and a simile, which fits the line of reasoning about the speaker becoming sharper. The explanation is still thin and does not examine "armed" or the image of darkness in much depth.
- Row C: "But the speaker never actually says his question out loud, saying he would "rather he said it for himself," so he is holding back too." - This touches on a real tension (the speaker's own silence as a kind of wall), which is a promising idea. It is only a single passing sentence and is not developed or sustained, so it does not reach sophistication.
- Row C: "it feels like the neighbor has the final word and the speaker does not answer him" - Notes that the repeated proverb frames the ending and goes unrefuted, but the conclusion mostly restates earlier points. The essay does not sustain a complex argument about the unresolved tension, so no sophistication credit.

Sample essay (low; scored 2/6: thesis 0, evidence 2, sophistication 0)
In the poem "Mending Wall" by Robert Frost, the speaker and his neighbor fix a stone wall between their land every spring. The poem is about walls and how people feel about them. The speaker seems to be against the wall but the neighbor is for it, and Frost shows this through different poetic techniques.

At the beginning the speaker says "Something there is that doesn't love a wall." This is personification because the something is given a feeling like love. It makes the reader think that nature wants the wall to come down. The speaker then describes how the wall falls apart and how he and the neighbor have to meet and fix it. They walk the line and each one picks up the boulders that fell on their side. This shows that they work together even though they are on different sides.

Later the speaker says it is "just another kind of out-door game." This shows he thinks the wall is not serious. He also talks about the pine trees and the apple orchard and says his apple trees will never get across. This shows that the wall is not needed. The neighbor only says "Good fences make good neighbours." He says this at the middle and again at the end of the poem, which is repetition.

At the end the speaker describes the neighbor like "an old-stone savage armed." This is a simile and it shows the speaker thinks the neighbor is stuck in the past and will not change his mind. The neighbor "will not go behind his father's saying." So in the end the speaker is against the wall and the neighbor is for it, and the poem shows how they disagree about it.
- Row A: "The speaker seems to be against the wall but the neighbor is for it, and Frost shows this through different poetic techniques." - Only says speaker is against and neighbor is for; names techniques without a claim about the speaker's divided attitude. No defensible thesis, so no credit.
- Row A: "So in the end the speaker is against the wall and the neighbor is for it, and the poem shows how they disagree about it." - Conclusion restates the same simple opposition and never recognizes that the speaker himself calls the neighbor to rebuild.
- Row B: "This is personification because the something is given a feeling like love." - Names a relevant device and gives a thin explanation of effect, but does not connect it to the speaker's own ambivalence.
- Row B: "This shows that they work together even though they are on different sides." - Mostly paraphrase of the plot; the shared work could support a divided-attitude argument but isn't developed or quoted.
- Row B: "He says this at the middle and again at the end of the poem, which is repetition." - Identifies repetition but does not explain its effect, such as the proverb getting the last word.
- Row B: "This shows that the wall is not needed." - Takes the speaker's mockery at face value and ignores the irony that he still initiates the repair; commentary stays surface-level.
- Row C: "it shows the speaker thinks the neighbor is stuck in the past and will not change his mind" - Some interpretation of the simile, but one-sided; no sense of the speaker's own tension or reliance on his own sayings, so no sophistication.

The speaker's teasing is a kind of wall of its own, since he would 'rather / He said it for himself' and never says his question out loud. The neighbor's proverb gets the last word, and the poem lets it stand without refuting it. An essay can also earn the point by weighing the gap between the speaker's warmth in the shared work and his condescension in the 'savage' simile. Merely mentioning that walls can be both good and bad, or adding outside political allegory, does not earn the point unless it is grounded in the text and sustained.

scoring_notes: Do not reward claims about Frost's biography or intentions beyond the text and headnote.
Treating the speaker as simply anti-wall, without dealing with his starting and joining the repair, usually limits Row B and blocks Row C.
Accept readings that sympathize with the neighbor if they are supported by evidence, such as the proverb's last-word position or the speaker's condescension.
Correct naming of device terms is not required. Reward accurate explanation of how a choice works.
The speaker's quoted words to the neighbor (lines 30 to 36) are imagined speech he says he 'could' use. Responses that notice that he never says them earn credit for precision.

defensible_positions: The speaker mocks the wall as useless, yet he is the one who calls the neighbor to rebuild it, so his skepticism lives alongside real attachment to the ritual and to the contact it allows.
The speaker's playful, mischievous tone hides real judgment: by the end the neighbor appears as an 'old-stone savage armed' who 'moves in darkness,' a shift from teasing to unease.

The poem sets two inherited sayings against each other, the speaker's 'Something there is' and the neighbor's proverb, which suggests that the speaker is also bound by belief and that neither man fully reasons for himself.
The wall is both a divider and the only thing that brings the two men together, so the speaker's attitude is divided because the wall both separates them and connects them.
The speaker's refusal to say his objection out loud ('I'd rather / He said it for himself') builds its own barrier, which complicates his criticism of the neighbor's closed mind.

devices.quote: Something there is that doesn't love a wall
devices.effect: Giving a vague, unnamed force its own will makes the speaker's opposition to the wall seem natural and almost mystical, while also hiding that it is his own wish.

devices.quote: I let my neighbour know beyond the hill;
devices.effect: The man who questions the wall is the one who starts its repair, which shows his divided attitude.

devices.quote: We keep the wall between us as we go.
devices.effect: Repeating 'between us' from the line before stresses that the shared work is also a separation. They cooperate only from opposite sides.

devices.quote: Oh, just another kind of out-door game,
devices.effect: Calling the repair a game makes it look trivial and fun, which shows the speaker's amused distance but also his enjoyment of the shared activity.

devices.quote: He is all pine and I am apple orchard.
devices.effect: The speaker defines the two men by their trees, a contrast that supports his argument that no wall is needed while still marking how different they are.
The neighbor's repeated proverb frames the second half of the poem and gets the last word, showing his unshaken certainty and the speaker's failure to change it.
Comparing the neighbor to a primitive armed figure turns the speaker's teasing into condescension and a sense of threat.

devices.quote: He moves in darkness as it seems to me,
devices.effect: The darkness stretches from literal shade to mental darkness, while 'as it seems to me' admits this is only the speaker's view.

devices.quote: Spring is the mischief in me
devices.effect: Calling his challenge 'mischief' frames it as play rather than conviction, which shows his unwillingness to argue seriously.

common_pitfalls: Reducing the poem to a simple conflict in which the speaker is right and the neighbor is wrong, and ignoring the speaker's part in rebuilding the wall.
Treating 'Good fences make good neighbours' as the poem's moral, or as the speaker's own belief, without analysis.
Summarizing the wall-mending scene instead of analyzing how specific choices show attitude.
Missing that the speech in lines 30 to 36 is only imagined and never said to the neighbor.
Applying outside political or historical allegory about borders that the text does not support.
Listing devices without connecting them to the speaker's divided attitude.

samples.essay:
In "Mending Wall," Robert Frost's speaker spends most of the poem making fun of a wall that he himself calls his neighbor out to repair every spring. That contradiction is the center of the poem. Through quiet irony, the playful language of games and spells, and a late turn toward darker imagery, Frost presents a speaker who sees himself as the free thinker of the pair but who is just as tied to the wall as his neighbor is. In the end his teasing works as a wall of its own.

The poem opens with a riddle instead of a statement: "Something there is that doesn't love a wall" (line 1). The inverted syntax holds back the subject and makes the line sound like an old country saying. That mysterious "Something," which "sends the frozen-ground-swell under it," gives nature a will, and the speaker clearly sides with it. Only a few lines later, though, he admits, "I let my neighbour know beyond the hill" (12). The flat, plain wording of this line is the irony. The man who seems to be on the side of the gaps is the one who sets up the repair. Frost doesn't point this out. He just puts the two ideas close together and lets the reader see the gap between them. The repeated phrase "between us" in lines 14 and 15 sharpens the point, because the two men are working side by side and sharing a "we" even as the wall they are building keeps them apart.

The speaker handles this tension by turning the work into play. He calls it "just another kind of out-door game, / One on a side" (21-22), which makes the hard labor of lifting boulders sound like a sport with teams. Even his spell, "Stay where you are until our backs are turned!" (19), is half a joke, but it also shows him joining in a ritual instead of standing outside it. When he finally argues, his logic is concrete and a little smug: "He is all pine and I am apple orchard" (24). The neighbor answers with a proverb, and the speaker blames his own urge to question on the season, saying "Spring is the mischief in me" (28). Calling it mischief rather than conviction lets him avoid committing to his own argument. Most of his challenge is something he only wonders about saying, and he holds back the word "Elves" because he would "rather / He said it for himself" (37-38). So he wants the neighbor to tear down the wall, but he won't say so plainly himself.

The playfulness disappears near the end. The speaker sees his neighbor holding a stone in each hand "like an old-stone savage armed" (40). With this simile the neighbor stops being a partner in a game and becomes a primitive fighter, and the stones turn into weapons. The image of darkness goes further: "He moves in darkness as it seems to me, / Not of woods only" (41-42). The literal shade of the pines becomes a metaphor for ignorance, and "his father's saying" (43) suggests that the neighbor's certainty was handed down to him, not thought out. Still, the hedge "as it seems to me" admits that this judgment is only the speaker's view, and the condescension says as much about him as it does about the neighbor.

What keeps the poem from being a simple victory for the speaker is that he has his own refrain too. He repeats "Something there is that doesn't love a wall" in line 35, and it sounds as inherited and as unexplained as "Good fences make good neighbours." He mocks blind repetition while doing it himself. Frost also gives the neighbor the last line, and the proverb stands with no answer. The speaker never really wins the argument, because he never fully makes it. His division is left unresolved. He resents the wall, looks down on the man who believes in it, and still meets him at the line every spring.

samples.essay:
In "Mending Wall," Robert Frost shows a speaker who is of two minds. He makes fun of the wall and of his neighbor, but he is also the one who calls the neighbor every spring to fix it, so he is part of the thing he questions. Frost uses personification, tone, and imagery to show this divided attitude, which gets sharper toward the end of the poem.

The poem begins by saying "Something there is that doesn't love a wall." This is personification, since the force that knocks the wall down is given feelings, and it makes it seem like nature itself is on the speaker's side against the wall. The line is repeated later, which shows the speaker keeps coming back to this idea. But right after, the speaker says "I let my neighbour know beyond the hill." This is ironic because he is the one who starts the mending. He complains about the wall, but he still keeps it going each year, so he does not fully believe his own argument.

The speaker also treats the work as playful. He calls it "just another kind of out-door game," and he uses a "spell" to make the stones balance. These details make the tone light and teasing, and they show he enjoys working with his neighbor even though he thinks the wall is pointless. The phrase "between us" is repeated, which shows that the wall separates them but they are also doing the job together. The contrast between "pine" and "apple orchard" is used to prove his point that the wall is not needed, since his trees will never bother the neighbor's.

However, the tone changes near the end. When the speaker sees the neighbor "like an old-stone savage armed," the simile is not friendly anymore. It makes the neighbor seem primitive and a little dangerous. The speaker also says the neighbor "moves in darkness," which is an image that suggests the neighbor is not thinking clearly, only following what he was taught. The speaker looks down on him for this. But the speaker never actually says his question out loud, saying he would "rather he said it for himself," so he is holding back too.

The poem ends with the neighbor repeating "Good fences make good neighbours," the same line from before. Because it is repeated, it feels like the neighbor has the final word and the speaker does not answer him. This shows the speaker cannot fully shake the neighbor's certainty even though he thinks he is smarter. In the end, Frost uses these techniques to show that the speaker is both against the wall and part of it, and that he is both amused by his neighbor and bothered by him.

annotations.quote: he is also the one who calls the neighbor every spring to fix it, so he is part of the thing he questions
annotations.comment: Defensible thesis: it names the speaker's divided attitude (mocks the wall yet starts the repair) and previews the techniques. It is somewhat general about how the poem shows the division, but it answers the prompt, so it earns the thesis point.

annotations.quote: This is personification, since the force that knocks the wall down is given feelings
annotations.comment: Names a technique and gives a specific quotation, with some explanation of effect (nature on the speaker's side). The commentary is brief and does not tie the personification closely to the speaker's ambivalence.

annotations.quote: This is ironic because he is the one who starts the mending.
annotations.comment: Uses a key piece of evidence ("I let my neighbour know") and explains how it shows the speaker undercutting his own argument. This is good, relevant commentary, though it stays at one sentence of analysis.

annotations.comment: Evidence from "game" and "spell" is used, but the commentary is general ("light and teasing") and does not explore how the half-serious spell connects to the Elves or to the speaker's own reliance on sayings. The pine and apple point is only summarized.

annotations.comment: Good identification of a shift in attitude and a simile, which fits the line of reasoning about the speaker becoming sharper. The explanation is still thin and does not examine "armed" or the image of darkness in much depth.

annotations.quote: But the speaker never actually says his question out loud, saying he would "rather he said it for himself," so he is holding back too.
annotations.comment: This touches on a real tension (the speaker's own silence as a kind of wall), which is a promising idea. It is only a single passing sentence and is not developed or sustained, so it does not reach sophistication.

annotations.quote: it feels like the neighbor has the final word and the speaker does not answer him
annotations.comment: Notes that the repeated proverb frames the ending and goes unrefuted, but the conclusion mostly restates earlier points. The essay does not sustain a complex argument about the unresolved tension, so no sophistication credit.

samples.essay:
In the poem "Mending Wall" by Robert Frost, the speaker and his neighbor fix a stone wall between their land every spring. The poem is about walls and how people feel about them. The speaker seems to be against the wall but the neighbor is for it, and Frost shows this through different poetic techniques.

At the beginning the speaker says "Something there is that doesn't love a wall." This is personification because the something is given a feeling like love. It makes the reader think that nature wants the wall to come down. The speaker then describes how the wall falls apart and how he and the neighbor have to meet and fix it. They walk the line and each one picks up the boulders that fell on their side. This shows that they work together even though they are on different sides.

Later the speaker says it is "just another kind of out-door game." This shows he thinks the wall is not serious. He also talks about the pine trees and the apple orchard and says his apple trees will never get across. This shows that the wall is not needed. The neighbor only says "Good fences make good neighbours." He says this at the middle and again at the end of the poem, which is repetition.

At the end the speaker describes the neighbor like "an old-stone savage armed." This is a simile and it shows the speaker thinks the neighbor is stuck in the past and will not change his mind. The neighbor "will not go behind his father's saying." So in the end the speaker is against the wall and the neighbor is for it, and the poem shows how they disagree about it.

annotations.quote: The speaker seems to be against the wall but the neighbor is for it, and Frost shows this through different poetic techniques.
annotations.comment: Only says speaker is against and neighbor is for; names techniques without a claim about the speaker's divided attitude. No defensible thesis, so no credit.

annotations.quote: So in the end the speaker is against the wall and the neighbor is for it, and the poem shows how they disagree about it.
annotations.comment: Conclusion restates the same simple opposition and never recognizes that the speaker himself calls the neighbor to rebuild.

annotations.quote: This is personification because the something is given a feeling like love.
annotations.comment: Names a relevant device and gives a thin explanation of effect, but does not connect it to the speaker's own ambivalence.

annotations.quote: This shows that they work together even though they are on different sides.
annotations.comment: Mostly paraphrase of the plot; the shared work could support a divided-attitude argument but isn't developed or quoted.

annotations.quote: He says this at the middle and again at the end of the poem, which is repetition.
annotations.comment: Identifies repetition but does not explain its effect, such as the proverb getting the last word.

annotations.quote: This shows that the wall is not needed.
annotations.comment: Takes the speaker's mockery at face value and ignores the irony that he still initiates the repair; commentary stays surface-level.

annotations.quote: it shows the speaker thinks the neighbor is stuck in the past and will not change his mind
annotations.comment: Some interpretation of the simile, but one-sided; no sense of the speaker's own tension or reliance on his own sayings, so no sophistication.

blueprint.central_idea: The speaker questions the wall and the neighbor's inherited proverb, yet he starts and joins the yearly rebuilding. His teasing skepticism turns into unease about the neighbor's closed mind, while the poem quietly suggests that the speaker relies on sayings and builds barriers of his own.
blueprint.complexity: Division and connection are tangled together: the wall separates the men and is also their only shared ritual, and the speaker's playful tone both hides and reveals judgment. The neighbor's refrain gets the last word without being refuted, so the poem leaves open whether the speaker's skepticism is wiser or just another set of fixed habits.
